items.title: Batman: Caped Crusader Season 2 Review - Darker, Deadlier, but Still Flawed
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of Batman: Caped Crusader Season 2. All 10 episodes of Season 2 will premiere on Prime Video on Friday, July 31.

Batman: Caped Crusader may be the latest in a long lineage of Batman-themed animated series, but its appeal has always been crystal clear. It’s a project that not only brings Batman: The Animated Series co-creator Bruce Timm back to the forefront, but one that allows Timm to work wholly unencumbered by the technological and content limitations that hindered the original BTAS. This is an adult-oriented show that fully leans into the violence, sex, and film noir roots of the Batman franchise. The results continue to be well worth a watch in Season 2, even if the series tends to settle for being different from BTAS more than actually trying to be the superior product.

Season 2 moves forward from its predecessor’s Harvey Dent-focused storyline as Batman (Hamish Linklater) confronts an even more ominous era in Gotham City. The fight to take down resilient crime boss Rupert Thorne (Cedric Yarbrough) is further complicated by the emergence of new Gotham City power players like Riddler (Ronan Raftery) and the enigmatic Joker (Matthew Needham). More than ever, the Dark Knight needs a few good friends by his side, something he’s still learning to accept in Season 2.

The thing about Caped Crusader is that it’s strangely disinterested in Batman himself. That’s a criticism that’s often been overblown when leveled against the various live-action films, but here it certainly holds water. Compared to the many villains and supporting characters on display in the series, Bruce Wayne and his alter ego come across as bland and almost psychologically inert. For a guy who gets his kicks dressing as a bat every night, that’s certainly a choice on the part of Timm and the writers. It’s an issue that is only compounded in Season 2, which keeps Bruce at an even further remove because he’s no longer being psychoanalyzed on Harley Quinn’s (Jamie Chung) couch. Thanks mostly to Linklater’s solid vocal performance, the series is great about drawing a distinction between billionaire playboy and grim vigilante, but it very rarely cuts to the genuine person who exists at the intersection of those two personas. Only Episode 3 strives for something deeper with Bruce.

Ultimately, though, that’s only a significant problem when you don’t consider the utter glut of Batman media on the market. If a more complex psychological portrait of the Dark Knight is what you’re after, there are other, better avenues to explore. Caped Crusader is very clearly more interested in delving into the psychology of the Bat rogues and the supporting cast.

There, Season 2 is largely much more successful. The series places a real premium on allowing viewers to understand and empathize with many of these characters, whether it’s crusading defense attorney Barbara Gordon (Krystal Joy Brown), the righteously vengeful inventor Roxy Rocket (Wunmi Mosaku), or the mentally unstable Rose Canton (Fryda Wolff). I’m perhaps most impressed with the show’s continued handling of Detective Flass (Gary Anthony Williams), a character who’s elevated from one-note bad cop in the comics to a genuinely intriguing figure. Batman himself may be an implacable presence in the series, but so many of these characters exist as complex mirrors of his psyche.

One also has to credit Timm and company for not simply replaying the hits from BTAS when it comes to the antagonist characters. Nearly every villain feels fundamentally different in terms of appearance and background. At times, these characters come across as different for the sake of being different. Take someone like Hattie Tetch (Laraine Newman), a gender-bent version of Mad Hatter who’s so far removed from the source material she might as well be an original character. But for every Hattie, there are several iconic villains who receive major and enjoyable overhauls in Season 2. And there are some returning favorites, for good measure. Chung’s Harley Quinn is once again central to one of the best episodes of the season.

But what of Riddler and Joker, the two characters who form the twin backbones of Season 2’s serialized narrative? Suffice it to say, Caped Crusader finds far more success with one than the other. Like Hattie, Eddie Nygma is distorted to the point of being almost unrecognizable. His love of puzzles and mind games is seriously downplayed. Instead, the show depicts him as a raving psychopath who “riddles” his victim with bullets. None of the fascinating intellectual rivalry between Batman and Riddler is on display here, eliminating the entire point of the latter character in the process.

But Joker is another matter entirely. The show takes its sweet time putting this character into the spotlight (as you’d expect), but once it does, Season 2 really hits its groove. As evidenced by the villain’s dour, shadowy appearance, this is a version of Joker almost wholly inspired by the early Golden Age comics and actor Conrad Veidt’s character Gwynplaine in 1928’s The Man Who Laughs. He’s not a preening trickster or comedian, but a brooding terrorist who holds Gotham entirely in thrall.

Unlike Riddler, Joker never feels different for the sake of being different. He’s simply drawing from a slightly different well than we normally see in Batman media. The character also benefits from an excellent performance by Needham, who brings just the right sort of quiet yet zealous attitude the role demands. He may spend much of the season staring ominously from the shadows, but Joker’s belated presence helps elevate the final few chapters of the season in a major way.

Visually and musically, Caped Crusader still exists in the shadow of its parent series. It makes the most of Timm’s iconic aesthetic, and generally beats out the animation quality seen in DC’s various direct-to-video films, but there are flaws to be found. The series is almost too clean at times. The figures lack the same grimy texture that permeates the environments, and many of the CG-animated vehicles look a bit odd in motion. And while Frederik Wiedmann’s moody orchestral score does its job nicely enough, never does it reach the heights of Shirley Walker’s work on BTAS. That’s sort of the common theme with Caped Crusader. It’s a different and more intensely noir-flavored answer to Batman: The Animated Series, but not necessarily superior.

items.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Tom Holland’s run as Spider-Man has been nothing if not consistent. Three solo MCU outings and three supporting appearances leading up to and including Avengers: Endgame have shown Marvel Studios and the Russo Brothers struck gold in casting Holland back in Captain America: Civil War, identifying a guy who has scant few detractors out there thanks to how well he’s able to embody both Peter Parker and Spider-Man. Peter’s struggle to find balance between those poles, as it so often does with Spidey, proves to be the main thrust of Spider-Man: Brand New Day. After Shang-Chi and Wonder Man, director Destin Daniel Cretton scores a hat trick by keeping the next chapter of Peter’s journey a lot more restrained than his latter, cosmically-charged outings, even with telepathic threats and organic web fluid oozing from his wrists in play.

Right out of the gate, it must be said that, as Spidey’s first MCU movie set almost entirely within Manhattan: it’s real good to have New York City so front and center in Brand New Day’s action. It’s part of a more-focused mission statement for the movie that Cretton makes immediately in the opening montage, a swing-and-punch medley which covers the last few years of Peter’s lonely life in a world that has completely forgotten who he is thanks to Doctor Strange’s spell at the end of No Way Home.

With no personal life to cultivate, Peter has been laser-focused on cleaning up the city, and his success has gained him the trust of Detective DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas) and the rest of the NYPD, leading to enough operational latitude to drive crime in New York to an all-time low. That progress comes at the cost of Peter forgoing all connection, but a chance spotting of Ned (Jacob Batalon) convinces him to attend a party to see whether that spark between him and not just Ned, but MJ (Zendaya) still lingers somewhere in their subconsciouses. The unexpected emotional turbulence that comes with that is what triggers the physiological changes which threaten to subsume the Peter we all know and love, which manifest as supercharged versions of his existing powers, as well as brand new ones like organic web-shooters.

Brand New Day sees Holland at his best in the moments where maybe, there’s some lingering recognition on the faces of his former friends. His yearning for that old, familiar feeling comes through when the story needs it to, leading to some effective gut punches when things go wrong for him. He’s just as sharp as ever under the mask, too. Peter’s life may be in a rut, but Spider-Man has a lot more swagger thanks to his winning streak as a crimefighter. As his abilities go haywire, that greater power also effectively animates Spidey’s sense of responsibility to the fallout of his actions in some sobering moments. The stakes of Peter’s heroism are a lot different when Iron Man and Doctor Strange aren’t around to clean up his messes, after all.

There’s not quite enough that sets apart Brand New Day’s drama of struggling to serve dual identities from previous Spider-Man movies, and so Holland doesn’t have room to break into new territory with the character.

While MJ’s function to the plot doesn’t amount to much more than being a weakness of Peter’s for Sadie Sink’s antagonist to exploit, Zendaya does make space for herself to refine MJ’s established mix of acerbic wit and empathy for others into what feels like a real progression for the character. There’s a fullness to how MJ embraces the odd circumstances that come with Peter’s return into her life, and Zendaya does a great job servicing the nuances of that in her scenes with Holland. Those two, they’ve got some chemistry, don’t know if you’ve heard.

Peter’s eternal struggle to grapple with power and responsibility is reflected in Sink’s mysterious nemesis, who I’m thrilled to reveal, is of course, as we all anticipated, a reincarnated MODOK, everyone’s favorite Avenger. Sink doesn’t truly enter the action until the middle of the movie, but she runs away with the second half on the strength of her quiet fury and a pretty cool power set to back it up. This character’s ability to body-hop between different hosts proves a reliable trick that Cretton deploys liberally across not just the fight scenes, but during chases and even some more dialogue-heavy moments. It’s not too dissimilar from how we’ve seen Loki’s powers used in the past, but given Peter’s vulnerable state, it’s a strong enough incentive to keep him second-guessing whether reaching out for help is really safe.

Following Jon Watts’ work on the “Home” trilogy, Destin Daniel Cretton handles the passing of the directorial torch well. Brand New Day tends towards being a little on the nose with some of its musings on evolution and identity, but if Cretton paints with a broad brush, at least his lines are clean. The director’s proven instincts for acrobatic action keep Brand New Day similarly light on its feet. This is as “Spider-Man” as Tom Holland’s Spidey has ever felt in combat not just thanks to the increased level of his abilities, but in how precisely Cretton moves the camera to capture all that spectacle.

And yes, Spidey does some Insomniac-coded stuff during the fights. And yes… it’s cool to see a well-loved adaptation of the character from a different medium get a knuckle bump from the big dogs at Marvel Studios in that way.

Bringing Spider-Man back down to ground and recontextualizing him into the considerable, interwoven world that Marvel Studios has endeavored to build out is mostly a success here. Sure, if you were one of those folks who was hoping to see Scorpion (Michael Mando), Tombstone (Marvin Jones III), or Boomerang (computer generated man) get their due as fleshed-out baddies, you’ll be dismayed to discover they aren’t used as much more than set dressing here. The rogues gallery is mostly waved aside this time, but Brand New Day gets plenty of mileage out of calling in previously-established MCU characters to help Spider-Man along his friendly, neighborhood way.

Mark Ruffalo’s Bruce Banner / Hulk is a sensible choice for a character to pluck out of the roster to bounce science jargon off of, but even more effective as an authority on Peter’s deliberations over how much control he should be trying to exert over nature as it takes its course. That said, it’s Jon Bernthal’s Frank Castle / Punisher, with his own long history of isolating through tragedy, who really finds the most success among the returning MCU faces. If Tony Stark was a father figure to Peter, Frank’s more of a hot-blooded uncle, and the chemistry the two actors share is a reliable source of chaotic, argumentative energy that serves the movie well. You have to have a little context for who The Punisher is for all that to have its full effect, but that is the Sacha Baron Cohen-faced Mephisto with which you bargain when you buy a movie ticket to any new Marvel.

Less successfully deployed from the MCU toy chest is the Department of Damage Control, whose Director Bill Metzger (Tramell Tillman) entreats Spider-Man to help them stop the mystery antagonist testing the boundaries of their facilities for weaknesses like a body-hopping raptor. Damage Control has been consolidating power for years at this point in the MCU - not usually a chill thing to do in these movies - and their stated goal of turning dangers into buffers those very dangers isn’t convincingly conceived enough or followed through on to give the normally charismatic Tillman much room to leave an impression. Brand New Day’s overreach with Damage Control extends into some odd choices with respect to who it’s choosing to “reform.” Metzger highlights the purportedly redeemed ninjas of The Hand as exemplary of his approach early on, but in a way that positions the group that once terrorized The Defenders as a group of wayward kids who just needed some structure in their lives. Though there are some undeniably great action beats involving them, they never rise above feeling like bright red enemies for Spidey to knock around to get some experience points.

Though Brand New Day occasionally fumbles the execution of how it pushes forward some of these more minor elements of the larger MCU tapestry, it does a pretty solid job of keeping the amount of “homework” it has to do setting up future franchise entries to a respectable minimum. The new elements established, thunderclouds on the horizon, are both relevant and removed enough from Peter’s focus here as not to distract from the conflict at hand. Whether all that’s expressly in service of the character or because Avengers: Doomsday is right around the corner and there’s nothing for Spider-Man to do about such massive threats right now, Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s smaller scope is a welcome change of pace after a string of high-concept adventures. It’s… it’s almost like… a Spider-Man homecoming.

items.title: Xgimi Titan Noir Pro Review
items.author: Bo Moore
items.content:
In the market, Xgimi has been making a name for itself with compelling lifestyle projectors that offer competitive projection alongside stylish designs that better blend in with home decor than the ugly plastic boxes coming from many other brands. With the earlier Titan, Xgimi tested the prosumer waters. Now, the Titan Noir family finds a middle ground, offering something for enthusiasts who want superb projection (and more screen size than a standard 4K TV) in a living room-friendly package. The Titan Noir family includes the Titan Noir ($3,999), Noir Pro ($4,999) and Noir Max ($5,999) with the key differences between each model being their brightness and contrast ratio. Xgimi sent over the middle sibling for testing, and whether for watching movies or gaming on the big screen, it downrights rocks.

Xgimi Titan Noir Pro – Design and Features

The Xgimi Titan Noir Pro is a looker. Xgimi has shown a knack for fairly elegant-looking lifestyle projectors that step away from the dated designs that look more at home in an office. The Titan Noir Pro follows that trend, combining smooth metal and stylish grilles. It looks less at home on a coffee table than some of Xgimi’s other models, but it’s still somewhat tame for a high-end home theater projector.

It’s also shockingly small and light for a projector delivering as much as it does. I’ve tested models like the Epson LS12000 and Sony Bravia Projector 7, and those things were units that took up a huge swathe of my mantle and took some care to heft up there. By contrast, the Titan Noir Pro is only 9.1 inches tall, 11.3 inches deep, and 14.9 inches wide, and some of that size comes from the metal legs it stands on. It’s also just 16.75 pounds, and that frankly feels almost too light for a projector aiming to provide so much brightness.

Aside from the legs that the Titan Noir Pro stands on, it’s a tame design. It’s really just a box with various vents for air intake and exhaust, a couple of speakers directly in the front. The lens sits off to one side at the front flanked by a few extra sensors for handling things like autofocus, auto keystone, and an eye-protection tool that dims the output when someone is in front of the laser projection. That last feature is useful, and this model has a special version that tries to only dim the light around where it detects a person’s head, though it doesn’t do a great job compensating when lens shift has been used on the projection.

One major advantage for the Titan Noir Pro is its optical system. The optics of the projector offer zoom and lens shift to a considerable degree (throw ratios range from 0.98:1 to 2.0:1, and the projection can shift 50% horizontally or 130% vertically in either direction). This makes it possible to set the projector in one spot and shrink and move the projection to where it fits quite easily without sacrificing a single pixel. By contrast, many projectors advertise convenient automatic screen alignment but do so digitally, cropping the projection to fit and lowering the resolution you see as a result.

On the back of the Titan Noir Pro are most of the ports you’ll need. There are three HDMI ports. One of them offers eARC for audio, though there’s also a 3.5mm and an optical audio output port. There are two USB-A ports for local media or powering streaming sticks. The projector includes a LAN port and Wi-Fi connectivity, though you might not get much use out of either because the projector lacks Google TV or the like.

Xgimi does include a large styrofoam carrying case that’s helpful for protecting the projector on the go and keeping its remote and power brick all together. That power brick is unfortunately very large and heavy. It would have been convenient to have the power supply integrated into the projector, but I’ve begun to suspect some brands keep them external on premium products like this so they’re easier to replace in the event of failure.

The remote included is also helpful. It provides simple controls for easy navigation of the settings and offers backlighting on a few of the primary buttons. The remote also includes four customizable shortcut buttons that let you quickly access specific settings you’ll use often. The volume buttons are easy enough to feel out in the dark of a home theater, but both the volume and shortcut controls don’t get any backlighting.

Xgimi Titan Noir Pro – Software

Many of Xgimi’s projectors come with a built-in streaming OS like Android TV or Google TV, but not the Titan Noir Pro. It somewhat feels like it has Google TV built-in, because a lot of the menus are similar, but that’s all the operating system handles: settings menus. This means you’ll need to connect video sources (or a USB drive) to get anything out of the projector, but it also makes for a very responsive system that allows for quick changes to settings and faster bootup.

It might have been nice to see a fuller operating system baked in, but in a time when LG monitors are delivering adware and operating systems are plugging large banner ads on startup, I’m starting to think that maybe the better default is actually to include one. Xgimi could have at least provide a landing screen, perhaps with previews of each HDMI input source, which can be helpful when you – like me – never remember which device is connected to which HDMI port.

One setting I wish the projector supported is the option to skip HDMI 1 as an input source. That port handles eARC audio output, so there’s a good chance it will be used for audio output exclusively in many setups, but the projector still lets you select it was an input source even when it’s handling eARC (sure, some eARC audio devices can also pass through video, but I don’t think most are used in that way), Since HDMI 1 is the first input source the projector boots, too, it won’t be useful at all for folks who just have that connected to their sound system.

Xgimi Titan Noir Pro – Gaming and Performance

The Xgimi Titan Noir Pro is simply brilliant. I’ve been using and testing projectors for a long time, and the Titan Noir Pro may be the most well-rounded and capable model I’ve put my hands on.

To start, its adjustable optics make a perfectly sharp picture easy to get without having to fuss much with where the projector is positioned. Whether low on a coffee table, mid-way up the room on a desk, or perched high on a mantle, I could easily get the projector images squared away on my wall or projection screen using the zoom and lens shift controls. From there, autofocus can sharpen the image quickly and effectively.

Not needing keystone adjustments is huge, as these not only cut into the usable image but also introduce latency, and for gaming, that’s just unacceptable.

That said, the out-of-the-box defaults aren’t exactly the best. I’m always surprised to see high-end projectors like this come running heavy motion interpolation by default, and the Titan Noir Pro is no exception. It introduces unsightly artifacts and awkward motion in a lot of cases. If you’re gaming, the projector will likely automatically switch to game mode that disables this, but with a streaming stick connected, it doesn't.

The projection itself is simply stunning, though. The Titan Noir Pro is fantastically bright. I played through several 007 First Light challenges, including some that took place at night, even while light came in from outside my living room. I was content watching movies and TV without even turning off all the lights, too.

Of course, the Titan Noir Pro looks even better in a dark space. It’s normally too bright to actually use in a dark room (think lights out and blackout curtains in place). But it features a dual-iris system that can clamp down to reduce the overall light output while ramping up contrast. The result is a picture that still can dazzle with highlights while showing off a deep black floor. On a lot of projectors I’ve tested, I can see black letterboxes no matter what’s on-screen, but with the Titan Noir Pro, I could almost never see the letterboxes.

All the brightness and contrast comes by way of an RGB laser light source that simply dazzles when it comes to color output. While a projector may never match an OLED display in terms of contrast, RGB laser light sources offer simply staggering color gamut. The colorful scenery, costumes, and bending effects in the live-action Avatar: The Last Airbender show are stunning to see on the Titan Noir Pro. With support for HDR10+ and Dolby Vision, the Titan Noir Pro has you covered for high-end formats. It’s too bad it’s a little early for Dolby Vision 2 support.

Those visual chops come along for gaming, too. I played through hours of 007 First Light on the Titan Noir Pro, and it kept up brilliantly. The story beats were all rendered with cinematic flair, the projector making it seem all that much more like a movie. Latency was negligible while running at 4K/60Hz, but the projector can also drop down to 1080p/240Hz and enable VRR (AMD FreeSync Premium). In that setting, I smashed through the fast-paced action setpieces of the game with imperceptible input lag, making it easy to dash for cover and snap to enemy targets. I normally game on fast OLED monitors with keyboard and mouse, and gaming on the Titan Noir Pro didn’t feel like it held me back one bit. The has some similar capabilities at a lower price and will likely work well if you’re mostly after brightness, but the Titan Noir Pro’s black levels are on another level.

Alongside the great visual performance, the Titan Noir Pro is surprisingly quiet. Though it has a good deal of power to contend with, I never heard its cooling system even from a few feet away.

Impressive though the visuals may be, audio from the projector is nothing to get excited about. The speakers can put out a bit of volume, but they don’t create a sense of space, don’t have deep sub-bass, and are too focused in the mids, creating a harsh sound at high volume. They can do in a pinch, but you’ll absolutely want to pair the projector with speakers to get the most out of it.

Xgimi Titan Noir Pro – Testing

Analyzing a projector is a little more difficult than a display, since you can’t simply set up a colorimeter on the lens, and anywhere else the colorimeter will either block the light it’s meant to measure or capture ambient lighting as well. That doesn’t make it impossible to evaluate, but less precise. Still, with my colorimeter set up a foot in front of a 1.1-gain white projector screen, it measured the Titan Noir Pro at 93% coverage of the DCI-P3 color space and 85% of the BT.2020 color space. Having seen my fair share of ultra-colorful displays, I’d say those measurements are on the low side of what I’m actually seeing from the Titan Noir Pro.

Brightness is a little more direct to measure. I displayed a full white screen and averaged the brightness across nine points to find the Titan Noir Pro putting out 4,375 lumens. That was with the Standard picture setting and iris fully open, which thankfully doesn’t lead to a picture that’s overly blue or green as some projectors in their highest brightness modes do.

Contrast is more difficult to measure but not impossible. Switching to a test pattern for measuring contrast with two bright white squares in opposite corners and black everywhere else, I measured an average 4,870 lux for the white areas and just 5 lux for the black space, coming out to a 974:1 contrast ratio. That’s already incredible for a projector, but the Titan Noir Pro still has some moves to bust out.

With its iris shut down as far as possible, its brightness goes down considerably, but its contrast jumps. The same test produced an average 1,238 lux in the corners and 0.77 lux in the center for a 1,608:1 contrast ratio. Here is where we get to the challenge for epic projectors like this: you need to optimize the viewing area as well. A lot of light will bounce off your wall or screen, reflect throughout the room, and land right back on the screen, elevating the black levels. By blocking out most of the projection with a black velvet fabric that absorbed most of the light but had a center hole to allow some of the projected light through, I was able to measure the black center point at an even lower 0.19 lux with all settings otherwise the same as above. This would put the contrast at an exceptional 6,518:1 in a thoroughly light-controlled room.

Mark Knapp is a contributing freelancer for IGN covering everything electronics and gaming hardware. He has over 10 years of experience in the tech industry with bylines at PCMag, Reviewed, CNET, and more. Find Mark on Twitter

items.title: Rick and Morty Season 9 Finale Review & Recap: "Field of Dreams"
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Rick and Morty Season 9, Episode 10!

I wouldn't quite go so far as to say that Rick and Morty Season 9 saved its best episode for last. "Ricks Days, Seven Nights" is pretty hard to top. But "Field of Dreams" is still definitely a close second, and for many of the same reasons. This episode caps off the season with a very winning blend of high-concept humor and crushing existential drama.

This week, we get introduced to the concept of a Rick estate sale, where Rick's (Ian Cardoni) death leads his multiversal counterparts to swoop in and claim his stuff like opportunistic vultures. It's always fun seeing alternate versions of Rick and Morty (Harry Belden), especially now in this post-Citadel era. But ultimately, the whole estate sale thing is just a means to an end for the real meat of this episode, which is Morty's decision to go funeral-hopping.

It's both an amusing and disturbing concept. You can understand why Morty would be curious about how these various alternate families are grappling with his death, and how quickly he becomes addicted to the voyeuristic thrill of it all. And once he's inevitably caught in the act, you can even see why he would grow attached to a family that actually shows him love and appreciation. Even if the whole thing is incredibly toxic and destructive for all involved.

And that's why this episode works so well. Morty's seemingly benign thirst for affection becomes a weight that drags everyone down into darkness. This alternate Jerry (Chris Parnell), already a borderline abusive parent beneath the pleasant facade, loses his grip on reality when faced with the prospect of reclaiming his son. Rick morphs from recovering addict with a fulfilling home life to a mirror image of the drunken, spiralling mess we've come to know so well. The Russian janitor becomes a dog with an impossibly long neck. Everyone loses here.

There's a real but very grim appeal in watching as Rick rapidly throws it all away, less out of a desire to help Morty than the allure of becoming the man he might have been all those years ago. Along the way, this episode makes sparing but effective use of Malin Ackerman's character, another reminder of what Rick is throwing away in his reckless pursuit of science. The finale hits on some of the same ideas as "Ricks Days, Seven Nights" in terms of Rick escaping the emptiness of his life, only to fall completely back into that role, but it's done differently enough that it still feels novel here.

Special credit goes to Parnell here. One of the neat things about Jerry when it comes to these alternate universe episodes is that the various versions of him feel distinct in a way that isn't really the case for the rest of the Smith family. Part of that is down to the writing, of course, but don't discount Parnell's performance when he plays characters like this Jerry or the late Jerry Prime. It's such a far cry from the usual sad sack version of the character, which we really see in those couple of scenes with regular Jerry singing about his stupid fedora.

Episode 10 reaches a fittingly bleak end, resulting in the deaths of Rick, Jerry, and everyone else in Morty's false family. None of it mattered. Rick's entire quest to build a portal gun was a massive failure. But, hey, it's ok. Another Rick estate sale means Morty has an easy ticket home. So it is that the season wraps with a proper dose of existential angst, but this time coming from Morty rather than his grandfather.

items.title: House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 6 Recap and Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Farewell, Criston Cole, we hardly knew ye. Well, we enjoyed hating you in Season 1, mostly forgot you existed in Season 2 and have been reminded that you have some game this year, thanks to your adoption of both guerilla warfare and an air of gloomy resignation. Also, to give credit where it's due, thanks to a killer opening battle scene this time – and that was just the start of another really strong episode.

That opener, a battle called the Butcher's Ball, deserves real love: Criston (Fabien Frankel) and company walk into an ambush but outfight their opponents only to discover a second, larger trap springing around them. Cole proves that there’s more than one way to mace somebody and then, with the tiniest hint of nobility now, wraps Alicent’s (Olivia Cooke) token around his sword and offers to fight for his men's lives, but gets Boromir-ed instead – by Lady Alysanne Blackwood (Annie Shapero). That's a small change from the book, but a smart way of streamlining a few characters. It's also one less thing for Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy) to worry about – though Cole achieved his aim of slowing her Rivermen’s arrival at Tumbleton by weeks.

The rest of the episode can be divided roughly in three. There are the intertwining stories of Rhaenyra and Alicent, the many concerns of various Dragonriders, and the endless scheming of James Norton’s Ormund and company.

First, Rhaenyra and Alicent. The queen is furious at her ex-bestie for trying to escape, so Alicent decides that honesty is the best policy and confesses that Helaena (Phia Saban) is pregnant, pointing out the threat this must pose. Rhaenyra recognises the dynastic danger but still acts offended that Alicent didn't trust her. That’s rich given that, by the end of the episode, she's asked her former stepmother to go kill her son, Aemond (Ewan Mitchell). Maybe she should get off her high horse. Helaena is also furious at her mother for lying about bringing her toddler daughter on their escape, and is refusing to eat, so Alicent has serious issues to negotiate there as well.

Things are tough for Rhaenyra too: her council is still ungovernable, her husband Daemon (Matt Smith) a maverick, and the smallfolk are complaining directly to her in audiences that she consistently mishandles. She has started to act, which is a step up from her passive father, but her political instincts are undeveloped and unreliable – and she makes one mistake here that could prove costly.

Rhaenyra has started to act ... but her political instincts are undeveloped and unreliable – and she makes one mistake here that could prove costly.

Meanwhile lots of dragonriders are suffering. Baela (Bethany Antonia) is still pushing herself to exhaustion, looking for Vhagar and redemption after the Gullet, though she finds time to snog Alyn (Abubakar Salim). That’s smart time management, since he’s really stepped up as a leader and counsellor, and is also a babe. Her sister Rhaena (Phoebe Campbell) is still on the verge of madness in the Vale with her wild dragon Sheepstealer, surviving on scraps and running afoul of Lady Jeyne Arryn (Amanda Collin) for flying out in search of Baela. Aegon (Tom Glynn-Carney) is busy burying his murder victim from last week – or at least watching Tyland Lannister (Jefferson Hall) do it for him, and still musing about the negative 360-performance review he received from his underling Larys (Matthew Needham). And Aemond is debating his next move in Harrenhal, unsure how far to trust Alys (Gayle Rankin) until he decides to tryst her instead. She counsels waiting, saying he’s hidden as long as Vhagar stays away – but she doesn’t know that Helaena’s visions have revealed his hiding place to Rhaenyra.

Ulf (Tom Bennett) is increasingly miserable about his long days on watch at Tumbleton and being confined to the Red Keep when in King’s Landing; Daemon finds him wandering the city and sharply orders him back into confinement. And Hugh (Kieran Bew) mugs a farmer for his clothes and cart in order to visit his wife (Ellora Torchia) in Tumbleton, who offers an ice cold welcome where he expected open arms. As she sees it, he abandoned her to search for his own glory; he says he thought only to assure their safety. They’re both a little bit right, and it’s heartbreaking. Finally, Daemon is stalking King’s Landing trying to track down the Gold Cloaks’ killers after his entire police force resigned. He succeeds in ambushing the ringleader we saw last time, but it does no good: they’re a hydra, and there’s always someone else to rise up. Ormund’s seeds of chaos are bearing great fruit in the capital.

And that brings us to the man himself, the Blofeld-ian author of all Rhaenyra’s pain – or at least the bits she hasn’t brought on herself – Lord Ormund Hightower. He’s lecturing Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) as usual with pearls of wisdom like, “The common man as a rule is of no interest or concern” and “Rhaenyra will not burn her own subjects. She is a woman. Squeamish.” (Is this the same guy who lectured Daeron on the formidable and distinctly -squeamish Meria Martell last week?) He’s also withering and homophobic to Gwayne (Freddie Fox), one of the more straightforwardly likeable people in the show – though he apologises after Gwayne saves his life from a delegation of assassins that Rhaenyra dressed as Baratheon envoys. That was a dangerous move on her part: House Baratheon had been trying to sit the war out, and she may have forced them to pick Ormund’s side now that their House sigil has been so rudely abused.

Finally this week, Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint), who had just gotten over his snit at Rhaenyra and decided to return to King’s Landing to help her, was ambushed and (presumably) taken prisoner by Ormund’s right-hand man, “Bold” Jon Roxton (Joplin Sibtain). We’re getting deep into uncharted territory right now, even for book readers. No spoilers, but in George R.R. Martin’s source novel Fire & Blood, Gwayne did not outlive the late Ser Luthor, while Corlys was never captured by the Greens. Ormund has proved a wildly effective strategist in a way that Rhaenyra simply is not, and it’s becoming clear that the civil war was far from over when she took back the Iron Throne. Its blades still cut her arms when she takes her seat, but that might soon be the least of her problems. As Ormund shares his plans with Gwayne at the end of the episode, it’s obvious that we’ve only seen a fraction of what he’s up to.

items.title: Cape Fear Episode 9 Recap and Review – ‘The Scar’
items.author: Michael Peyton
items.content:
Spoilers below for Episode 9 of . New episodes stream every Friday on Apple TV.

Cape Fear Episode 9 is a mess. Whereas the last few entries of the show have been propulsive and mind-bogglingly chaotic, the latest episode of the Apple TV series - titled “The Scar” - commits the cardinal sin of being boring.

Sure, there are a few wild moments (No Natalie! Don’t have sex with your maybe-sister in prison in order to steal her hidden cell phone!), but “The Scar” is otherwise a featherweight filler episode premiering right when the series needs to be firing on all cylinders.

, she was driving like a bat out of hell away from Savannah to find Max’s sister Crystal in North Carolina. When she arrives at the Cape Fear River, there’s no sign of Crystal, so Anna heads over to Max’s father’s house. Once there, she confronts Max’s father and stepmother (who seems to be so far gone that she’s given a doll - who she believes is her daughter Crystal - to nurse).

Later, Anna gets drunk at a local bar (it seems she’s fully off the wagon now) and passes out. She comes to the next morning on Crystal’s houseboat where, over breakfast beers, the two women have a long conversation about Max (this episode fails the Bechdel Test spectacularly).

Crystal reveals that she took all of the many, many photos of Max as evidence of his misdeeds and to prevent him from “coming after” her. She reveals that Amy - the woman who killed herself in the season premiere at Max’s behest - had her life together before Max showed up, which leads Crystal and Anna to take a short trip over to Amy’s trailer.

Back in Savannah, Tom, Natalie, and Zack are still in various states of incarceration. Natalie gets hassled by a fellow inmate before Nevaeh comes to her rescue with a nicely-timed chair to the aggressor's head.

Meanwhile, Max pays Tom a visit and warns about a “gift” he’ll receive in his cell later. All the while, Zack is practically nowhere to be found. The show’s underuse of Joe Anders in the back half of the season is immensely frustrating given the actor’s wonderful turn in earlier episodes. Apart from a brief phone conversation with Tom, Zack (and Anders) barely has any screentime this episode yet again, which robs the show of one of its best characters.

At the jail where Natalie is being held, the episode reaches a low point. In a phone call, Nevaeh (who somehow has a hidden cell phone) has an unconscionably clumsy conversation with Max that quickly resolves many of the season’s major mysteries and answers multiple long-simmering questions with unprompted exposition and absolutely no build-up. During the conversation we find out definitively: A) Max has been manipulating Nevaeh; B) she’s been his direct accomplice the whole time; and C) part of Max’s endgame is to have Nevaeh kill Natalie so that Anna “can feel the pain” of losing a child like Max did.

Soon after, Natalie, who suspects something is awry, attacks Nevaeh and then immediately starts making out with her. After the two have sex (somehow without any of the prison guards noticing), Nevaeh continues the parade of exposition by confirming to Natalie that Max told her to break into the Bowdens’ house, spike their tea with acid, seduce Zack, and make him bite off his own toe.

And thus, many of the most provocative threads of the entire show are quickly resolved. It’s a shame that the resolution of these storylines wasn’t handled with the same care with which they had been built to this point.

Back in North Carolina, Crystal and Anna break into Amy’s trailer, where Anna finds a picture of a boy with a scar running down his entire side. When Anna asks Crystal about the photo, she storms out. Anna, deducing that the boy is Crystal’s son, catches up with her and gets Crystal to admit that she gave the boy away because “she was a mess.”

In Savannah, Max pays Noa a visit and tries to threaten her into revealing Anna’s location. For a moment, you’re pretty sure Noa’s going to bite it, but Max abruptly leaves after seeming to have somehow snagged whatever information he needed without murdering Noa.

Across town in grown-up prison, Tom receives his mysterious gift from Max - a package containing a cell phone and a noose. Max later calls Tom and tries to convince him to hang himself, just like Tom’s brother hanged himself decades prior. Distraught, Tom calls Anna to say he loves her.

Afterward Tom receives an “official” prison-to-prison phone call (boy, is this guy on the phone a lot for an inmate) where Zack’s doctor reveals that Zack has escaped from the psychiatric hospital. Back at Natalie’s jail, Noa arrives to bail out Natalie, who’s stolen Nevaeh’s secret phone. It looks like Daddy’s little henchman has finally been neutralized.

On the houseboat, Anna searches for a recording of conversations between Amy and Max. When Crystal tries to lock her below deck, Anna pulls a gun on her and goads Crystal into confessing that it was in fact she, and not Max, who killed Max’s wife and son. It’s another major revelation that falls completely flat due to absolutely no build-up or tension.

Anna then calls Max and tells her that she knows about Crystal, and how she suspects that the boy with the scar was in fact fathered by Max. Soon, Max’s creepy father and the weird kid who tried to kiss Natalie in a previous episode arrive and disarm Anna. Anna soon realizes that the kid, named Luke, is the boy with the scar from the photo and incites a family argument on the boat deck. In the commotion, Anna jumps overboard and begins to swim away just as Max arrives.

All of this builds to what one would assume would be a tense final showdown between Max and Anna and a resolution to their melodramatic feud. It should be a moment of anticipation, but instead lands with an absolute thud.

There are still glimpses of hallmarks that have made Cape Fear such a wild, rich roller coaster throughout the entire season. The cinematography and scenery are breathtaking. Many of the actors are still turning in first-rate performances. But “The Scar” is barely half an episode of storytelling, with major moments that feel rushed and long-awaited explanations that are oversimplified.

Episode 9 of Cape Fear could have been a huge episode for the show, setting the stage for a climactic confrontation between the show’s leads in a fight to the death for the ages. Instead, we’re left with a muddled, watered-down episode that hopefully is an aberration before next week’s finale.

items.title: Samsung S90H OLED TV Review
items.author: Bo Moore
items.content:
I've been reviewing TVs for the better part of five years now, and few lineups have impressed me as consistently as Samsung's S90-series. Having tested several generations of the OLED, it's become the TV I most often recommend to buyers who want flagship OLED performance and don't mind giving up Dolby Vision. Year after year, Samsung has found ways to squeeze more out of the mid-range panel without reinventing the formula, making the S90 line one of the safest bets in premium TVs, particularly for gamers.

The Samsung S90H OLED TV doesn't stray far from that winning blueprint, but that's hardly a criticism. Building on last year's model with a brighter, more refined panel, a 165Hz refresh rate borrowed from last year’s flagship , and all the gaming features you'd expect from a modern OLED, it's another incredibly capable all-rounder. The biggest hurdle this time is price. At $1,699 for the 55-inch model I tested, the S90H is a significant investment in a time when saving is utterly crucial. Fortunately, after spending several weeks with the set across movies, streaming, and gaming, I came away convinced the improvements are substantial enough to justify the premium.

Samsung S90H – Setup & Design

Samsung’s TV setup was always fairly simple, but it’s been streamlined into a total breeze. The dual feet simply slide into place and lock without the need for a screwdriver or any additional tools, making it one of the easiest TVs I’ve assembled in recent memory. You then simply pop on the pedestal part to the feet and it’s good to stand up on your entertainment system, but I would’ve appreciated a few more built-in cable management touches around the back.

Once powered on, Samsung’s SmartThings app handles most of the heavy lifting. Pairing the TV to Wi-Fi, signing into Samsung services, and connecting compatible devices takes just a few moments all on your smartphone, eliminating much of the usual setup friction. It’s the kind of process that gets you watching content instead of tapping through endless menus. I also love that you can upload and save your home page settings, so if you ever need to upgrade or already live inside the Samsung ecosystem, everything is right there for you on startup.

The 55-inch S90H model I tested is remarkably slim and surprisingly light at around 38 pounds (17.3 kg) with its stand attached, making it easy enough for one person to maneuver during setup. The chassis measures just under 1.6 inches thick at its deepest point, giving it an elegant profile whether it’s sitting on a media console or mounted to a wall.

Around the front, Samsung keeps distractions to a minimum. The bezels aren’t completely invisible, but they’re thin enough to disappear once content starts playing. The overall design feels understated rather than flashy. It lets the panel be the star of the show, which is exactly what an OLED should do, and even more impressive is that anti-glare matte finish that cuts through nasty reflections with ease.

Powering everything is Samsung’s NQ4 AI Gen3 Processor, which handles 4K AI Upscaling Pro, motion processing, and Samsung’s suite of AI picture enhancements. Navigation throughout Tizen feels as snappy as ever, apps launch without hesitation, and switching between HDMI inputs is quick. The Tizen OS has seen several improvements, which makes navigation so much simpler. More importantly, the processor never feels like it’s getting in the way – it keeps the interface responsive while leaving you free to decide how much of Samsung’s image processing you actually want enabled.

Samsung has also quietly improved Tizen over the past few generations. Gone is the older side-panel interface, replaced by a cleaner home screen that keeps apps, inputs, and settings organized across the top of the display. It still takes a little time to learn where everything lives, but once you do, navigation feels faster and far less cluttered than it used to. My only real annoyance is Samsung's optional Daily Board and Ambient features, which can greet you with weather updates and smart home information whenever you walk by the display. It's a clever idea, but one that can feel unnecessary if you're walking through the living room a lot.

I tested the 55-inch Samsung S90H OLED over the course of several days using a mix of movies, games, and calibration software. Alongside everyday viewing, I measured the TV using Datacolor’s SpyderPro in four configurations: Standard Mode (SDR), Filmmaker Mode (SDR), Standard Mode (HDR), and Filmmaker Mode (HDR). Testing focused on brightness, contrast, white point, gamma/EOTF tracking, color gamut coverage, and Delta-E color accuracy to compare Samsung’s default image processing against its creator-focused picture mode.

For real-world performance, I paired the TV with a Panasonic DP-UB820-K 4K Blu-ray player for physical media, a PlayStation 5 Pro, gaming PC, and Nintendo Switch 2, while also evaluating streaming content through Samsung’s built-in Tizen platform. Movies spanning modern HDR releases, classic DVDs, and streamed content helped evaluate everything from HDR presentation and OLED black levels to upscaling and motion handling.

The Samsung S90H OLED is a reminder that impressive hardware doesn't always translate into an impressive out-of-the-box experience. Beneath Samsung's processing sits an outstanding OLED panel capable of exceptional contrast, rich color, and plenty of brightness, but its default Eco and Standard picture modes are the biggest culprits behind the disappointing image quality many first-time buyers may experience.

If you simply unbox the TV and leave everything at its defaults, the S90H delivers the kind of image Samsung has become known for on showroom floors: bright, vivid, and immediately attention-grabbing. During testing, Standard Mode reached 411.8 nits in SDR, proving the S90H isn't shy with its luminance. The problem is that Samsung aggressively manipulates nearly every aspect of the image.

The most obvious example is white balance. As brightness increased, the measured white point climbed from 8,900K at the lowest setting to an icy 11,900K at full brightness. Since films, television, and games are typically mastered around the D65 reference point of roughly 6,500K, that shift introduces an increasingly cool, blue-tinted image – something Samsung users may know all too well. Whites lose their neutrality, skin tones become less lifelike, and scenes that should feel warm instead take on a colder appearance.

That's only part of the story. Standard Mode also alters gamma to brighten shadows and midtones beyond what content creators intended. While that makes dark scenes easier to see in a brightly lit room, it also strips away some of the depth that makes OLED displays such a compelling buy in the first place. Rather than letting perfect black levels create natural contrast, Samsung opts to reveal more of the image, flattening scenes that should feel moodier or more atmospheric. Samsung's motion smoothing, sharpening, and AI enhancements are also enabled by default, and while they're easily disabled, most owners won't venture into those settings on day one.

Those shortcomings became easy to spot once I started watching actual content. on 4K Ultra HD disc looked spectacular regardless of picture mode, but Standard Mode immediately pushed the film's iconic neon-soaked cityscapes further than they needed to go. Blues and cyans became noticeably cooler, while bright signage and reflections carried more intensity than I felt the source intended. It still looked undeniably impressive, but there was a subtle artificiality to the image in Standard Mode that became difficult to ignore once I switched over to Filmmaker. Likewise, intimate hearing room scenes exposed the same tendency with skin tones. Faces took on a slightly cooler complexion under Standard Mode, and while the image never looked outright bad, it lacked the natural warmth and nuance Christopher Nolan's cinematography is known for.

The calibration results reflected what I was seeing. Standard Mode produced an average Delta-E of 21.95 in SDR, indicating colors regularly deviated well beyond their intended values. HDR was even more aggressive, with an average Delta-E climbing to 24.65. In practical terms, the colors on-screen often become different shades entirely.

Thankfully, switching to Filmmaker Mode changes the conversation. Samsung managed to achieve excellent color accuracy without sacrificing brightness. In fact, Filmmaker Mode measured slightly brighter in SDR during testing, reaching 428.6 nits while simultaneously bringing the white point back to a much healthier 6,200K to 6,900K range. That gives the image a far more natural appearance. Skin tones regain warmth, whites stop looking artificially cool, and the picture no longer feels like it's trying to impress you at every opportunity. Instead, it simply lets the OLED panel and director’s intent speak for themselves.

Filmmaker Mode isn't entirely flawless, however. Samsung still trends ever so slightly cooler than the D65 reference, though it's minor enough that most viewers are unlikely to notice. More apparent is the tradeoff introduced by the TV's excellent anti-glare coating. It does an excellent job of diffusing reflections and makes daytime viewing far more comfortable than many glossy OLEDs, but it also introduces a subtle softness to the image. Side-by-side with a glossy panel, the S90H doesn't quite have the same razor-sharp appearance, though it's a compromise I was more than willing to make given how great the TV looks even in my bright living room.

That restraint became especially apparent during opening flyover of New Port City. Against the OLED's perfectly black night sky, neon advertisements remained vibrant without bleeding into one another, while subtle gradients in the darkness stayed intact instead of being overwhelmed by exaggerated highlights. Even the film's darker sequences, like Major's thermoptic camouflage and the museum confrontation with the Puppet Master, retained remarkable shadow detail without sacrificing the depth OLED displays are famous for. proved equally revealing in a completely different way. The film's close-up dialogue scenes highlighted just how much more lifelike skin tones became in Filmmaker Mode, while the black-and-white sequences maintained clean grayscale transitions with excellent contrast and no obvious clipping in brighter portions of the frame.

HDR follows a similar pattern. Standard Mode unlocks more of the panel's raw color volume, measuring 93% DCI-P3 coverage compared to Filmmaker Mode's measured 75%. On paper, that sounds like an easy win for Samsung's default preset, but color volume only matters if those colors are being reproduced accurately. on Prime Video illustrated that difference particularly well in its vibrant reds and greens against the ink-black backdrop of space. Brilliant stars, spacecraft lighting, and reflective metallic surfaces all carried plenty of impact in both modes, but Filmmaker Mode rendered them with noticeably more restraint, avoiding the exaggerated, almost showroom-like appearance Standard Mode occasionally introduced. The result was a more convincing image, although the limitations of a compressed streaming source were still apparent in some darker gradients. The S90H does an admirable job minimizing those shortcomings, but it can't invent detail that simply isn't there.

Perhaps the biggest surprise, though, was the S90H's upscaling. Watching Ridley Scott's on DVD could have easily exposed the weaknesses of a modern 4K display, yet Samsung's processor handled the aging source with confidence. Compression artifacts weren't scrubbed away with heavy-handed noise reduction, film grain remained largely intact, and Osaka's rain-soaked streets retained far more texture than I expected from a standard-definition disc. There were still moments where compression noise and ringing peeked through – as they inevitably will with an older DVD – but Samsung wisely avoids overcorrecting. It's the kind of performance that makes revisiting an older movie collection far more enjoyable on a 55-inch 4K OLED.

Just as importantly, gamma tracking closely followed the BT.1886 reference curve, preserving shadow detail without artificially brightening it. OLED panels don't need help producing convincing contrast, and Filmmaker Mode wisely steps back and lets the hardware's perfect blacks create the depth naturally. Motion handling is equally impressive once Samsung's default smoothing is dialed back. Films retain their intended cinematic cadence without introducing distracting soap opera effects, though extremely slow camera pans can still exhibit the faint stutter that's characteristic of OLED's near-instantaneous response times.

Filmmaker Mode proved that point clearly. HDR color accuracy improved dramatically, with average Delta-E dropping from 24.65 to just 3.75 while the display tracked the HDR ST.2084 EOTF far more closely. The result is an image that looks less exaggerated but significantly more believable, with smoother gradients, more convincing highlights, and colors that appear faithful to the source rather than enhanced for effect.

It's also worth noting that HDR brightness measurements through SpyderPro should be viewed in context. Consumer OLEDs employ automatic brightness limiting, and HDR testing through Windows introduces additional variables that consumer calibration software isn't specifically designed to overcome. While those limitations can affect absolute HDR brightness readings, they don't change the broader takeaway from the testing: Samsung's processing has a much larger impact on picture quality than the panel itself.

That's ultimately what defines the S90H OLED TV. Samsung has once again built an OLED that hides its best qualities behind the wrong default settings. Spend thirty seconds switching into Filmmaker Mode and cutting out some of the AI-assisted features, and you're rewarded with one of the most balanced OLED images in its class, delivering rich HDR, excellent SDR performance, and some of the best out-of-the-box accuracy I've measured from Samsung.

Samsung has spent years building some of the best gaming TVs on the market, and the S90H OLED TV continues that tradition. Equipped with four HDMI 2.1 inputs that feature Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM), and a maximum refresh rate of 165Hz – a beefier number first introduced on last year's flagship Samsung S95F – the S90H feels purpose-built for gamers who want to squeeze every ounce of performance from their hardware. That said, Samsung still hasn’t copied the USB-C video output found on the Hisense U8 Mini-LED TV, a feature I’d love to see on more displays. Plus, there’s still no HDMI 2.2 input, but hopefully TVs will start to pick that up by 2027.

On , everything I threw at the S90H looked superb. showcased deep contrast during nighttime drives through Los Santos, while HDR highlights from headlights, streetlights, and sunsets popped against the OLED's perfect black levels without looking overprocessed. benefited from the panel's strong shadow detail, preserving environmental textures inside dimly lit vaults and abandoned buildings, while delivered smooth camera pans and crisp player animations throughout fast-paced matches. Motion remained clean across the board, and I never noticed distracting ghosting or blur during extended play sessions.

PC gaming proved equally impressive, thanks largely to the fact that the S90H is equipped with both AMD FreeSync and Nvidia G-Sync compatibility. Running Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced and in 4K highlighted just how striking Samsung's OLED panel can be when paired with modern HDR effects, but it was that really demonstrated the benefit of the S90H's 165Hz refresh rate. Fast-paced mech combat remained exceptionally responsive, with fluid camera movement and razor-sharp motion that made high frames feel genuinely worthwhile. Whether navigating menus or diving into chaotic battles, the TV always felt quick to respond.

Even the looked fantastic in 4K despite its more modest hardware. benefited from the OLED panel's rich colors, while looked vibrant without becoming oversaturated. It's a reminder that the S90H can elevate practically every platform you connect to it, even without the quantum dot filter on its more expensive flagship model.

If gaming is your primary focus, I'd have no hesitation recommending the S90H over many of its OLED rivals. Samsung's continued omission of Dolby Vision might sound like a disadvantage on paper, but it's largely irrelevant for PlayStation 5 Pro and Switch 2 owners, as those consoles don’t support Dolby Vision gaming anyway. That means you're getting outstanding HDR performance, a higher refresh rate than many competing OLEDs, excellent gaming features, and one of the most responsive gaming experiences available today without giving up much.

It's funny how a TV's quality is often best judged by people who don't spend their days reviewing them. My daily driver is still a projector, but after a few weeks with the S90H OLED, one of my friends stopped mid-conversation to ask what TV I was using because it “looked incredible." That's the power of Samsung's OLEDs. They don't just disappear into the background, but have a way of making people notice them, even when the screen’s turned off.

If you're shopping for a premium OLED TV and gaming is anywhere near the top of your priority list, the Samsung S90H is an easy recommendation. Its excellent panel, outstanding gaming feature set, and dramatically improved image accuracy in Filmmaker Mode make it one of the most well-rounded TVs Samsung has produced. It isn't a set that demands hours of tweaking or professional calibration to look its finest, simply switching away from the default Eco and Standard picture modes unlocks an image that's bright, cinematic, and impressively faithful to the source.

The biggest consideration is price. At $1,699 for the 55-inch model, the S90H OLED asks for a considerable investment, and that alone may push some buyers toward older models or competing OLEDs that frequently see aggressive discounts, like the LG C-series. At the time of writing, the , the S90H’s closest competitor, sits as low as $1,499 on Amazon. While it’s not quite the same, offering just 120Hz and no matte anti-glare coating, it’s always been the best value option for most buyers.

Even so, after living with the S90H TV for several weeks, I came away feeling that Samsung has made meaningful improvements where they matter most. The brighter panel, 165Hz refresh rate, refined processing, and exceptional gaming performance all add up to a TV that's easy to recommend, and one that continues the S90 series' reputation as my go-to OLED for most buyers willing to overlook the lack of Dolby Vision.

items.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 Review So Far
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
Samsung has been making its foldables for eight generations now, and while the company has tacked on the ‘Ultra’ branding to the Fold 8, the Flip 8 isn’t all that different to its predecessor. The main difference this time around is that it’s using a more powerful processor, and the price has gone up by $100.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 is packed with the same Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip that’s powering both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and the S26 Ultra. I haven’t had a chance to really put this phone through its paces yet, but just swapping to this high-end SoC, rather than the MediaTek chip in last generation’s model, should make the Flip 8 a much better gaming phone than last year’s version.

If you’ve ever seen any iteration of the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip, the Flip 8 will look incredibly familiar. When the phone is closed, you can interact with a 4.1-inch display that’ll let you run most, but not all apps. You can then open it up to a full 6.9-inch display, albeit with a bit of a narrower aspect ratio than most phones.

Out of all the foldables I’ve used, this type of form factor has always been the most novel to me. There’s just something about being able to fold a phone up into a little square that fits into whichever pocket or purse I’m using that day. It does help that Samsung’s Flip phones have been getting thinner every year too.

The Flip 8 is no different, shrinking down to 6.1mm when unfolded, which is down from the Flip 7’s 6.5mm. That’s not a huge difference, and you probably wouldn’t even notice the difference when the phones are next to each other, but it does let Samsung call it the ‘thinnest Flip yet,’ I suppose.

Both displays are AMOLED panels, with the outer display having a resolution of 1048 x 948, along with a 2520 x 1080 inner display. The pixel density of 391 ppi isn’t by modern smartphone standards, especially considering that the $799 Moto Razr has an incredibly similar display, albeit with a weaker chipset.

Like with any foldable, there is a crease in the middle of the inner display, but it is slightly less noticeable than it was on the Flip 7. I do notice it when I hold it at a certain angle, but in general with these foldables, it’s something my brain basically erases from my attention after a little while. The bigger problem on older foldables and, uh, flippables, was a gap between the edge of the crease and the rest of the chassis, which would allow dust to get in. Thankfully that’s not a problem anymore.

And just like with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, Samsung has added a new titanium alloy film and a titanium plate underneath the display, which should help prevent any damage from unfolding and re-folding the display, as well as make bending it backwards incredibly difficult. I didn’t actually test whether or not I could snap it in half, of course, but it should be pretty durable.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 has basically the same camera as the Z Flip 7, but it does include 2x optical zoom, where the 7 relied entirely on digital zoom. That was the biggest problem with last year’s flip, as the software-based ‘AI zoom’ wasn’t great at retaining detail.

I haven’t had the chance to go out and put the Z Flip 8’s camera through its paces yet, but Samsung is claiming that all of its foldables this year have much better night-time performance as well. However, I’ve never seen a smartphone come out that claimed to be good at night photography, so we’ll just have to wait and see.

For the longest time, the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip has always been a bit slower than the Fold, mostly due to size constraints. However, Samsung has found a way to shove the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 and 12GB of RAM into the Z Flip 8, so it should be able to hold its own against other smartphones. And, it really needs to hold its own, because at $1,199, it’s charging flagship money.

I’ve only had a few hours with the Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 8 so far, so I can’t say definitively how well it stacks up against the other phones I’ve tested with this chipset. But, it’s likely that it will lag at least a little bit behind something like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or the OnePlus 11, thanks to the heat constraints that come with a thinner chassis that’s essentially split in half.

I did play a bit of Arknights: Endfield on the Flip 8, and it performed just as well as the Fold 8 Ultra did. There is a caveat there, though: because of the lower display resolution, the game is quite a bit easier to run. Endfield tosses up a big, scary warning whenever you try to change the frame rate from 45 fps to 60 fps, but because the Flip 8 only has a 1080p display, it should be able to handle this higher setting, but it will get quite toasty.

Even when you’re not running experimental settings in games, the Flip 8 has some heating issues. In any game where you have to hold the phone horizontally, the outer display gets quite warm to the touch. It’s not hot enough to burn you or anything, but it does get uncomfortable if you’re holding it a while. On top of that, it just feels weird to have half the phone heating up, while the other side is relatively cool.

You probably won’t get much longer gaming sessions out of the Z Flip 8, anyway, though. This year’s model packs the same 4300mAh battery as its predecessor. That’s not the end of the world, after all there’s only so much battery you can fit in such a small phone, but it is a disappointment, especially considering that Samsung was able to upgrade the Fold 8 Ultra’s battery.

I need to spend a bit more time with the Galaxy Z Flip 8 before I can say anything for sure, but I love that Samsung packed it with a more powerful chip this time around. However, with the added power comes added heat, and I’ll have to see whether or not the Galaxy Z Flip 8 actually keeps performance churning over long workloads. That’s something that Samsung’s thinner phones have been struggling with for a while now, but if the throttling problem has been solved, the Galaxy Z Flip 8 could be a great gaming phone for anyone that doesn’t want a thick slab in their pocket all the time.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her

items.title: Motor City Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
will be released in theaters on July 24.

There are fewer than a dozen lines of audible, functional dialogue in Motor City — Potsy Ponciroli’s ’70s-set Venice Film Festival premiere — resulting in a gruff, stripped-bare action film that highlights the genre’s worst and best. That it comes down on the side of “highly entertaining” is a minor miracle, if only because Ponciroli and his cast are completely locked in to the moods and movements that dominate the screen, allowing for an unfiltered (if musically overbearing) piece with its own brutal rhythms.

Granted, when you sacrifice words in a movie that’s this reliant on minor details, you end up either focusing on bits of paper, like modern silent intertitles — foreclosure notices, job applications, news articles, and so on — or you end up forgoing information entirely. This applies to Motor City’s protagonist, John Miller, a hulking former soldier with a nondescript job and close crew-cut. However, when you have an actor like Alan Ritchson in the part (think Schwarzenegger with more sensitivity), it’s a sacrifice you can afford. The movie opens with Miller wreaking vengeful havoc, dropping a body on a speeding car from a rooftop before firing a shotgun while getting flung through the air.

It’s a blast, no pun intended, and it builds just enough curiosity for you to get with the pseudo-silent program when Motor City flashes back to several months prior. Miller, a lion-maned hustler on probation — again, those are all the details we have — proposes to his waitress girlfriend Sophie (Shailene Woodley) before being framed in a major drug bust. Through flashbacks and silent stares, we learn that the mastermind behind his false imprisonment is slimy drug lord Reynolds (Ben Foster), who has numerous corrupt cops at his disposal, like the leather trenchcoat-sporting Savick (Pablo Schreiber). Meanwhile, more clean-cut detectives like Ben McKenzie’s Kent seem intent on unraveling this conspiracy.

It’s in establishing these characters and their motives that familiar stock types and obvious costume design come in handy. Reynolds especially benefits from this, as well as from Foster’s casting as a skeevy, potbellied, envious ex, whose ploy is all about winning Sophie back. In the meantime, Miller languishes in prison, his hair and beard growing ever longer, and prepares to escape and exact revenge with the help of two former comrades on the outside: Youngblood (Lionel Boyce) and Singh (Amar Chadha-Patel).

The trio, who eventually stage a blazing clockwork prison escape, are pretty cool, albeit in familiar ways, what with their straight-from-a-soup-can swagger with which they strut away from explosions. However, this being a bog-standard revenge flick in every way (except its sound), you already know which characters are more disposable than others, which is to say “anyone who isn’t a white man.”

Still, Motor City makes for an engaging experience, if only because it forces its author and audience alike into a somewhat non-traditional mode of filmmaking and viewing. It shouldn’t be this out of the ordinary for an American action flick to depend on visual cues, but in an increasingly homogenized action landscape, watching body language, blocking, and editing tell a story is a delight unto itself. It certainly helps that the movie taps into visceral sensations along the way, such as its vicious bloodshed and one particularly exciting no-holds-barred combat scene in the confines of an elevator. All of this is enhanced by Ritchson and Foster delivering fully-committed performances as admittedly retrograde archetypes in pursuit of their blood feud over a woman.

Ritchson and Foster deliver fully-committed performances as admittedly retrograde archetypes in pursuit of their blood feud over a woman. 

If there’s one place Motor City drops the ball, however, it’s in its music selection. Any film that muffles and circumvents the spoken word is bound to rely on other auditory means, and while its ambient sounds are just fine — they’re functional and unremarkable rather than absorbing — the movie’s wall-to-wall needle drops in the vein of the Guardians of the Galaxy movies feel a touch random. The artists in question are certainly era-appropriate — David Bowie, Donna Summer, Fleetwood Mac, and so on — and they prevent boredom during the initial setup before the movie finally lets Steve Jablonsky’s booming score do its work. But the title is Motor City, and there’s nothing particularly Detroit-esque about it, least of all its tracklist: The Bowie song in question isn’t even “Panic in Detroit!” This was the era of Alice Cooper and Iggy Pop, and the birth of techno; you couldn’t ask for a more appropriately propulsive in-built soundtrack, and the movie doesn’t take advantage of any of it.

Ultimately, this ends up indicative of how even Motor City ends up part of the aforementioned homogenized traditions of American action films, where time, place, and music have an increasing unimportance. You can transpose the story to any other setting or era without losing all that much, which is disappointing. But regardless of its missteps, that the movie works at all is almost worth applauding, even if only for the fact that Ponciroli gets enough audio-visual basics right to craft a coherent film of wanton violence. It’s pretty silly and pretty fun.

items.title: Halo: Campaign Evolved Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
You can tell a single-player campaign is truly great when revisiting it sparks a similar joy as your very first run, even when you remember how it all plays out beat-by-beat. Pistol shots on scrambling Grunts, sticking Elites with plasma grenades, popping Flood like bubble wrap with an Assault Rifle; Halo: Campaign Evolved rekindled the familiar feeling of playing the original on a rented Xbox at my grandma's house in 2001. But as much as I adore Halo's campaign, with its simple yet thoughtful combat design, you can only play the hits so often. When the base game, the Anniversary Edition, and the Master Chief Collection are all readily available in 2026, it's easy to see this remake as more of an Unreal Engine test than anything. There’s a new batch of Skulls and three prequel missions to sweeten the deal, which are a fun few hours to blast through – but the changes outside the graphical overhaul are otherwise subtle, and as a whole, neither definitively improve nor detract from what I played 25 years ago. So, while it's great to see how well Halo has aged, we've been down this road many times before.

There aren't really any surprises here for those who've played Halo before; Master Chief awakens as the UNSC flagship is invaded by the alien Covenant and he escapes by landing on a mysterious ring-shaped planet. In its twists and turns through various biomes and chromed-out Forerunner halls, you uncover the truth about Halo itself, paving the way for the rest of the series. It's a clean, no-nonsense story that's refreshingly simple in retrospect. And let's not forget Master Chief, alongside Cortana, embodied the sentiment that , especially when you're going full speed in a Warthog as the classic theme song starts kicking in.

Campaign Evolved includes some brand-new cutscenes that teeter between kind of hokey to just . Pulling up to the beachfront in a Pelican for The Silent Cartographer has a little extra gravity but I do miss that original first-person fly-in, and the scene at the bow of the Pillar of Autumn for the opening mission kind of kills a sense of urgency. While these are efforts in being more cinematic and detailed with the story, they're sometimes missing the natural flow of they replaced.

Halo's combat calculus remains solid all these years later.

Overall, there's beauty in how quick Halo is to the punch, and it's this initial setup of a distinct sci-fi world that set the stage for some of the best designed shootouts of its era, which revolutionized first-person games on console at the time. The sense of wonder when trying to figure out which direction to go upon exploring Halo itself as Covenant ships constantly drop Grunts, Elites, and Jackals made for encounters that felt organic and varied. That mix of enemies alone was strong enough bread-and-butter for basic encounters, and when they're accompanied by armor-clad Hunters or cloaked Elites lurking with energy swords, I'm reminded that Halo was so much more than a scripted shooting gallery. And it's still a hearty challenge on Legendary runs, rivaling FPS campaigns of the modern day. As annoying as it may be to wipe from something like a pesky suicidal Grunt running around with two plasma grenades in-hand, you just have to accept it and play a little smarter next time. Positioning, grenade placement, and making the most of whatever weapons are available are part of why Halo's combat calculus remains solid all these years later.

Certain stretches do rely on repeat corridors for a little too long. Working your way through The Library alongside Guilty Spark, grinding through Covenant ship hallways, or backtracking during Two Betrayals; these aren't the most exciting parts of Halo. However, the fundamentals of its iconic, satisfying gunplay still make the repetition enjoyable at least. Moments like being able to take a Banshee or Scorpion tank through snow-covered valleys and approach open firefights with Halo's sense of freedom make the lulls a little more forgivable.
